posts.quote: THE HOT WATER BOTTLE WENT UNDER THE BLANKETS AT BEDTIME, AND BY MORNING IT WAS THE ONLY WARM THING IN THE HOUSE.
posts.caption: On the coldest nights, Mom filled the red rubber hot water bottle from the kettle and wrapped it in an old towel. It went to the bottom of the bed like a small stove, and you tucked your feet around it and didn't move. The bedroom had frost on the inside of the glass and a floor register that did nothing at all. By bedtime the blankets were piled so high you could barely turn over. By morning the bottle had gone lukewarm, and getting out from under all that weight was the hardest job of the day.
posts.first: Ours had a knitted cover Grandma made in a color nobody would have picked. I took it to my first apartment and it still had a slow leak at the cap. I kept filling it anyway.

posts.quote: THE VALENTINE BOX WAS A SHOEBOX IN CREPE PAPER, AND THE TEACHER MADE SURE EVERY KID GOT AT LEAST ONE.
posts.caption: The night before the class party, you sat at the kitchen table with a paper bag of cards and a pencil. Mom made you sign one for every name on the class list, including the boy who sat behind you and kicked your chair. The shoebox on the teacher's desk had a slot cut in the lid and red crepe paper wrapped around the sides. You carried it home at the end of the day and dumped it on the bed, and the little cards with the cartoon animals slid out in a pile. Somebody had quietly counted, so that nobody's pile was smaller than anybody else's.
posts.first: I still have a card from second grade with a cartoon pig on it that says I'M SWINE ABOUT YOU. I never found out who signed it, and I've decided it was the kid who kicked my chair.

posts.quote: Dad's pocket comb lived in his back pocket, and it came out for weddings, funerals, and every photograph.
posts.first: My father combed his hair one time a day, in the rearview mirror, right before he walked into church. The comb was black and worn smooth at the corners. I found one just like it in a drawer after he was gone and put it in my own pocket.

posts.quote: THE BUTCHER WRAPPED THE MEAT IN WHITE PAPER, TIED IT WITH STRING, AND WROTE THE PRICE IN GREASE PENCIL.
posts.caption: The butcher shop smelled like sawdust and cold, and the floor was swept so often it looked polished. He pulled a sheet off the big roll, set your pork chops in the middle, and folded the edges in three quick moves. Then the string came down from the ceiling dispenser, one wrap and a knot, and the end was snapped off against a little hook. The price went on in grease pencil, in numbers so square you could read them from across the counter. Mom carried it home against her coat like a parcel from somewhere far away.
posts.first: The butcher on our corner knew what my mother liked without asking and always set aside the thick end of the bacon for us. I remember the paper was slightly stiff and had a faint waxy shine. It folded so neatly you never needed tape.

posts.quote: THE TV TOOK A MINUTE TO WARM UP, AND THE WHOLE FAMILY STOOD THERE WAITING FOR THE PICTURE TO ARRIVE.
posts.caption: You turned the knob and nothing happened, and that was normal. First came a faint hum from somewhere in the cabinet, then a tiny white dot in the middle of the dark glass. The dot grew into a line, the line grew into a gray haze, and finally the picture swam up out of it. Dad stood with one hand on the dial like a man tuning a ship. Everyone else had gathered behind him already, as if the show might start without them.
posts.first: Our set was in a walnut cabinet with doors that closed over the screen, like a piece of furniture hiding something. When it warmed up, the whole living room got a little brighter. I can still hear that hum.

posts.quote: THE PHARMACIST / A MORTAR AND PESTLE, A GLASS COUNTER, AND A LABEL TYPED BY HAND
posts.caption: The pharmacist worked behind a high counter with a wall of brown bottles behind him. He knew your family doctor, your mother's allergies, and which of your cousins always came in coughing in March. A prescription took a few minutes because everything was counted out by hand onto a small tray. The label came out of a typewriter and was pressed onto the bottle with his thumb. Then he leaned over the counter and told you exactly when to take it, in a voice that was never in a hurry.
posts.first: Our pharmacist kept a jar of lollipops by the register for the kids, and he always asked how my grandmother was feeling before he asked what she needed. He knew the answer to both.

posts.quote: THE BARN CATS GOT A SAUCER OF WARM MILK AT MILKING TIME, AND NOT ONE OF THEM WAITED ANYWHERE ELSE.
posts.caption: Five minutes before the evening milking, the barn cats started to appear. They came from the hayloft, the feed room, and the machine shed, sitting in a loose half circle on the concrete like it was a meeting. Dad filled the pie tin with milk straight from the bucket, still warm, and they went at it without a sound. One cat always sat apart, sure that she was in charge. When the pan was empty they went back to being wild, and nobody on that farm ever called them pets.
posts.first: We had a gray tom who never let anyone touch him. He'd still sit exactly one arm's length away every night. My father called that friendship.

posts.character: Work and family (the pencil behind the ear)
posts.quote: The pencil behind Dad's ear was never sharp, and somehow it was never missing when he needed it.
posts.first: My father was a carpenter, and that stub of a pencil was flat on two sides so it wouldn't roll. He used it to mark a board and then set it back behind his ear without looking. I keep one in my workshop and put it in the exact same spot.

posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the telephone lineman)
posts.quote: THE TELEPHONE LINEMAN / A CLIMBING SPIKE, A LEATHER BELT, AND A POLE IN EVERY WEATHER
posts.caption: Every storm brought somebody up a pole. The lineman strapped on his leather belt, kicked in his climbing spikes, and walked up the trunk like it was a flight of stairs. He hung there, forty feet up, with a pair of pliers and a coil of wire, while the wind did what it liked. The whole street stood at their windows and watched, because their phone depended on him. When the line came back, there was a small click on the kitchen phone and Mom said, well, there he is.
posts.first: A lineman lived two doors down from us, and the kids thought he was a superhero in work boots. He let us hold his spikes once. They were heavier than they looked, and so was the job.

posts.quote: THE STADIUM BLANKET WENT OVER FIVE KNEES, AND THE COCOA WENT DOWN THE ROW TWICE.
posts.caption: By the second quarter, the metal bleachers were as cold as a skating rink. Somebody's mother had brought the big plaid blanket, and it stretched across a whole row of knees. The thermos made its way down the line, and everybody took a careful sip and handed it on. Out on the field the band was waiting at the end zone with their hats pulled down. Nobody remembered the score on the way home, but they remembered the blanket.
posts.first: My dad never missed a home game, even in years he knew a single person on the team. He kept a wool cap in the glove box just for those nights. I sat on a cold bench next to him and learned the names of everybody's mothers.
